title: You spent the night sleeping
hookLine: the night lost in sleep, the day in eating; a jewel of a life traded for a shell (Gauri M1, ang 156)

lines: NOTHING WENT WRONG. IT JUST WENT.
cards: Sunday night, ten o'clock. The weekend you'd been looking forward to since Wednesday is over. You slept late on Saturday.
A long lunch, then a nap, then dinner, and somehow it was Sunday afternoon. Try to name one thing from it you'd want to remember, and it takes a while. Nothing went wrong.
It just went. Guru Nanak looked at days like that five hundred years ago, and he priced them in the cheapest currency he knew.

teach.h: THE NIGHT IN SLEEP, THE DAY IN EATING.
teach.b: The shabad is in Raag Gauri, on ang 156. It begins, in effect: the night you wasted sleeping, the day you wasted eating. This life, precious as a diamond, is being traded away for a shell.
The word is kaudi, a cowrie shell.

In Guru Nanak's world, cowries were the smallest small change, the coin you'd barely bother to pick up. So picture a merchant walking into the market with a diamond and walking out with a cowrie, and calling it a day.
Then the refrain: you didn't come to know the Name of the Lord, and afterward, foolish one, you'll regret it. A fair note. Guru Nanak isn't against sleep, or food.

The Gurus lived as householders and ate with everyone in the langar. Elsewhere Gurbani speaks well of sleeping little and eating little, but the point here is sharper. Sleeping and eating aren't the waste.

The waste is when that's all a day becomes: one need met after another, and the diamond never spent on what it was for. In Sikh teaching, what it's for is naam, remembering the One, alongside honest work and sharing.
And notice the tone. It's not quite a scolding.

teach.h: A DIAMOND TRADED FOR A SHELL.
teach.b: It's the alarm of a friend watching you about to make a terrible trade: kaudi, a shell, for heera, a diamond.
Today is still in your hand, and the shabad asks you to look at it before you spend it.

how: Sikhs sing this Gauri shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its opening lines about a diamond life traded for a cowrie are often quoted as a call to remember the Name each day.

o: a cowrie shell, the smallest coin
a diamond, the worth of a life

games.q: the night and the day — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak says sleeping and eating are wrong
the waste is when a day becomes nothing else, and the Name is never remembered.
a cowrie shell was the smallest small change of the day
a diamond traded for a cowrie: the worst trade in the market.
the shabad says the trade is already final
it's a friend's alarm while the day is still in your hand.

games.q: you walk into the market with a diamond. what does Guru Nanak warn you're about to do?
o: trade it for a cowrie shell.
lose it on the way home.
games.why: the night in sleep, the day in eating: a diamond of a life traded for the smallest coin there is.

practice: Look ahead at the rest of today and find one hour that usually drifts away, on the phone, in front of the television, half-working, half-scrolling.

Decide, here, what it could be traded for instead, a walk with someone, a real conversation, a page of reading, some quiet remembering with Waheguru on the breath, and picture yourself spending it that way.
Notice how a single hour, chosen, feels heavier than three that just happen.

wordCard.voice: Kaudi, a cowrie shell, the smallest coin: Guru Nanak's warning, the night in sleep, the day in eating, and a diamond of a life traded for one.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a cowrie shell, the smallest coin; the life is traded for it.

carryVoice: Your line: not for a shell. A diamond deserves a better price. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Gauri Bairagan M1, Ang 156 (rain gavaaee soe kai)
